Write the model as syntax and fit it by maximum likelihood with no other package.
This is the first of five pages on the native engine.
Part of the [Models](models.html) collection.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Structure** | any path model you can write as syntax; this page uses simple mediation |
| **Class returned** | `SEMFit`, then `MediationData` from `extract_mediation()` |
| **Routes** | `fit_sem(syntax, data)`, or `fit_mediation(model = syntax, engine = "native")` |
| **Syntax** | `?"medfit-syntax"` lists every statement |

The five pages: this one (paths and defined parameters),
[a latent mediator](model-native-latent.html),
[constraints and the MBCO test](model-native-constraints.html), and
[several mediators and weights](model-native-multi.html), and
[categorical covariates](model-native-factors.html).

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(medfit)
library(generics)
```

These examples use the default listwise path. For the separate unreleased
three-variable FIML opt-in and its narrower support, see the
[native guide](native-guide.html#bounded-fiml).

## Fit it

Label a path with `name * variable`; `:=` defines a new quantity from labels and
gives it a delta-method standard error.

```{r}
#| label: fit
syntax <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment + covariate1 + covariate2
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment + covariate1 + covariate2
  ab := a * b
  total := cp + a * b
"
fit <- fit_sem(syntax, mediation_demo)
fit
```

`fit_sem()` returns a `SEMFit`. Read the defined parameters straight from it:

```{r}
#| label: defined
fit@defined
```

`summary(fit)` prints the full parameter table and the optimizer diagnostics.

## Get the usual objects

`extract_mediation()` turns the fit into a `MediationData`, so `nie()`, `tidy()`
and the bootstrap work as on any other page:

```{r}
#| label: extract
x <- extract_mediation(fit, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1",
                       outcome = "outcome")
class(x)[1]
tidy(x, type = "effects", conf_int = TRUE)
```

For one mediator, `fit_mediation()` does both steps:

```{r}
#| label: fit-mediation
x2 <- fit_mediation(model = syntax, data = mediation_demo,
                    treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1",
                    engine = "native")
nie(x2)
```

## Intercepts {#intercepts}

Since 0.15.0 every native fit has a mean structure by default (`meanstructure` left unset is `TRUE`), with a
free intercept for every observed variable you did not mention, as lavaan does with `meanstructure = TRUE`.
You write an intercept (`y ~ 1`, or `1` as a term, `y ~ 1 + x`) to restrict it or to give it a label.
The paths, variances and their standard errors are the same as without the mean structure; the fit
also reports the intercepts and the mean of each exogenous variable (fixed with the other
exogenous moments by default, so those rows have no standard error).

```{r}
#| label: intercepts-free
paths <- "mediator1 ~ a * treatment\noutcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment"
free <- fit_sem(paste0(paths, "\noutcome ~ 1"), mediation_demo)
tidy(free)[tidy(free)$op == "~1", c("term", "estimate", "std_error")]
```

An intercept you fix or constrain is a restriction, so it can change the other estimates.
Fixing the outcome intercept at 0 costs one degree of freedom, and `anova()` compares the
two fits:

```{r}
#| label: intercepts-fixed
zero <- fit_sem(paste0(paths, "\noutcome ~ 0*1"), mediation_demo)
c(free = free@theta[["cp"]], fixed_at_zero = zero@theta[["cp"]])
anova(free, zero)
```

Equating two intercepts works the same way (`i1 == i2` with labels `i1` and `i2`).
`meanstructure = NULL` fits a mean structure only when the model writes an intercept or a product (the 0.14.x
rule), and `meanstructure = FALSE` fits covariances only. A latent variable's mean is fixed at 0, and
a free latent intercept stops with "latent means are planned for a later release".
`extract_mediation()` reads the paths exactly as before; add a product term and it returns the
four-way decomposition ([below](#product-terms)).

## Compared with the `glm` engine

The two engines agree on the estimates and differ slightly in the standard
errors, because the native engine uses maximum-likelihood (not least-squares)
variances:

```{r}
#| label: compare
glm_fit <- fit_mediation(
  outcome ~ treatment + mediator1 + covariate1 + covariate2,
  mediator1 ~ treatment + covariate1 + covariate2,
  data = mediation_demo, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1"
)
rbind(native = tidy(x, type = "effects")$std_error,
      glm = tidy(glm_fit, type = "effects")$std_error)
```

## Product terms {#product-terms}

`x:m` (the colon, no spaces) on the right side of a regression is the product of two
observed variables, as in lavaan. The engine builds the column `x * m` from `data` after
listwise deletion and treats it as an observed exogenous variable, so the likelihood, the
constraints and the mean structure are the same as for any other regressor. `x:m` and `m:x` are one term,
stored under the canonical name (the two names sorted in the C locale, `m:x`), and a label
(`b*x:m`) names the coefficient. A product needs the mean structure, which is on by default. Writing the
treatment-by-mediator product in the outcome equation makes `extract_mediation()` return
the four-way decomposition; the
[interaction page](model-interaction.html#the-native-engine) runs a worked example,
including why centering the mediator matters.

```{r}
#| label: product
four <- fit_sem(
  "mediator1 ~ treatment
   outcome_int ~ treatment + mediator1 + mediator1:treatment",
  mediation_demo, se_type = "sandwich"
)
tidy(four)[1:4, c("term", "estimate", "std_error")]
```

The warning above says the global model test is not available for this model, because the product
contains the mediator, which is a regression target (details below). The coefficients and the sandwich standard
errors are unaffected.

A product is fitted only in the class below. Anything else stops, naming the feature, with a message
that says it is not yet supported with products; the same model works without the product. Each row
gives the limit and the start of its message.

| Limit | Message (starts with, or contains) |
|:--|:--|
| A space around `:` | "a product ':' needs a variable name on each side, written without spaces (x:m)" |
| `x:x`, `x:m:w` | "of a variable with itself is not supported", "a three-way or higher product" |
| A product as a left side (`x:m ~ y`, `x:m ~~ y`) | "cannot be a left side" |
| A product in `=~` or in a constraint expression | "is only valid on the right side of a regression" |
| A latent variable in a product | "products with latent variables are not supported in this version" |
| One product twice in an equation | "are the same product (canonical name" |
| A factor that is the target or downstream of it (`y ~ x + x:y`) | "(rule 8: no outcome-derived regressors)" |
| A loop of regressions | "The model is not recursive" |
| A residual covariance between outcomes | "A product model cannot have a residual covariance (rule 9)" |
| A label shared by two rows | "is used on more than one parameter" |
| A fixed coefficient | "has a fixed coefficient (rule 9)" |
| An inline bound on a coefficient or intercept (`lower(0)*x`) | "has a bound (rule 9" |
| `==`, `<` or `>` naming a coefficient label (`a < 1` too) | "names the coefficient label" |
| A fixed, shared or constrained intercept | "(rule 9, intercept clause" |
| `meanstructure = FALSE` | "`meanstructure = FALSE`, but the model has a product term" |
| A data column `m:x` that is not `x * m` | "is not the product of" |
| A product input that is not numeric, factor, character or logical (a date) | "needs numeric variables" |
| `information = "expected"`, endogenous factor | "is not available for a model with a product of an endogenous variable" |
| `anova()` or `mbco_sem()`, endogenous factor | "is not available for" ... "a model with a product term" |
| `extract_mediation()` with another product on the treatment or mediator | "the native extraction does not support the product" |

Two more facts are not errors. The covariance that completion would add between two pure
outcomes is fixed at 0 in a product model, with one note; and `fit_sem()` warns once when a
product is fitted without `se_type = "sandwich"`, which is the standard-error choice because a product
is not normal. `fixed_x = TRUE` fixes the product columns with the other exogenous variables.

The global chi-square is not valid when a factor of the product is itself a regression target (the model
treats the product as exogenous although it is a function of that variable), or when the exogenous
(co)variance block is restricted. `glance()` then reports chi-square, df and p-value as `NA`
with a note, and `anova()` and `mbco_sem()` refuse. A product of exogenous variables with a free block
keeps the ordinary test. [Methods and Formulas](methods.html#products-and-observed-information) gives
the reason.

## Limits

- **Observed means only.** A free latent mean or intercept stops with "latent means are
  planned for a later release"; the latent variable's mean is fixed at 0 (see
  [Intercepts](#intercepts)).
- **Constraints on an intercept** are checked up to a data mean about 1,000 times the standard
  deviation; beyond that the fit may stop with "no start converged". Constraints that leave
  every intercept free have no such limit.
- **A label must be defined** before `:=` can use it; an unknown label stops with
  "unknown parameter label".
- **Exogenous variables are fixed at their sample moments by default**, as lavaan does with
  `fixed.x = TRUE`: the structural estimates, their standard errors and the degrees of freedom do
  not change, the parameter count is smaller, and `logLik()`, AIC and BIC are conditional
  on the fixed variables, so fits with different fixed sets cannot be compared. The fixed rows stay in the
  parameter table without a standard error. `fixed_x = FALSE` estimates them (the 0.14.x default), and a
  vector of names fixes only those. AIC and BIC count the free intercepts and means; they equal a
  `lavaan::sem()` fit with `meanstructure = TRUE`, and exceed a default `lavaan::sem()` (no mean
  structure) by 2 per free intercept in AIC and by log(n) per free intercept in BIC.
- **AIC and BIC across product and no-product fits are not comparable.** The product column is an
  extra observed variable in the joint likelihood, so a fit with `x:m` and the same model without it
  describe different data (on `mediation_demo`, the same outcome gives AIC 2335.6 with the product and 2333.6
  without under the default settings; the gap can look small, but the two likelihoods are over different data). `AIC(fit_a, fit_b)`, `BIC(fit_a, fit_b)`, `anova()` and `mbco_sem()` refuse such a pair, naming the
  observed variables that differ.
- **Products** are limited to two observed variables inside the class in the table above; latent
  products, `x:x` and three-way products stop with the messages listed there.
- **Factor covariates** (a factor, character or logical column on a regression's right side) become
  0/1 dummies named `g_b`, `g_c` (reference: the first level), as `lm()` builds them. A label on the
  factor (`b*g`) stops; label one dummy (`b*g_b`). A factor as an outcome, a mediator or a four-way
  treatment is not supported, and `g:m` expands to one product per dummy (see `?"medfit-syntax"`).
- `summary()` reports diagnostics, including an improper solution and any active
  bound or constraint; read them before trusting a fit.

## The outcome ledger {#outcome-ledger}

`fit@diagnostics$ledger` records how the fit was reached: the optimizer state, likelihood and covariance status of
the fit and of each zero-product branch, with the notices raised on the way. An unresolved node is unknown, not
infeasible; only a literal contradiction between equalities is certified empty. A fit that cannot be trusted stops
with an error that carries the ledger as `$ledger`: see [errors that carry
evidence](guide-troubleshooting.html#errors-that-carry-evidence) and [how the branches are
built](computation-algorithms.html#a-zero-product-is-a-union-of-simpler-models).

## Stability {#stability}

The exported signatures of `fit_sem()` and `mbco_sem()`, the `SEMFit` properties and the model syntax in
`?"medfit-syntax"` change only through a deprecation. New syntax and new properties can be added: a name,
a table row or a property that exists today keeps its meaning. This matters for the features listed under
Limits (a categorical mediator or outcome, for example): they will arrive as additions, not as a rename of
`g_b`-style dummy names or of the `m:x` product name. A test (`test-api-freeze.R`) pins the current names.
Numerical fixes are not breaking changes.
